detail.longDescription: arXiv:2610.27258v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI advising systems are typically designed to always provide a response. Recent work has focused on developing systems that withhold advice in some instances, such as when advice quality is questionable, to improve the overall quality of guidance when it is given; a design paradigm we refer to as AI abstention. While substantial work has focused on optimizing when models should abstain, little is known about how users respond to systems that abstain. In a preregistered experiment, participants made repeated financial decisions, assisted by one of two advising regimes: an AI that advises selectively or one that advises on every decision. We find that the same AI abstention regime produces differential effects depending on the user: it increases advice acceptance among users with high perceived expertise and tends to decrease it among users with low perceived expertise. This differential effect is accounted for by the cognitive burden users face when repeatedly reconciling AI recommendations with their own judgment; AI abstention appears to relieve this burden among users with high perceived expertise, and in doing so increases their receptivity to advice. Further, AI abstention mitigates the decline in advice acceptance observed among expert users over repeated interactions. Exploratory evidence also suggests it increases appropriate acceptance where advice would improve the decision, increasing the downstream accuracy of perceived experts. The AI abstention regime is thus a first-order design property of AI advisory systems, and one that must be calibrated to the users a system serves.
